column1: Why do 3D graphics pipelines augment 3D vectors with a fourth homogeneous coordinate (w)?
column2: To represent translation, rotation, scaling, and perspective projection all as uniform matrix multiplications, which is impossible with pure 3x3 linear transforms alone.

column1: What geometric property distinguishes affine transformations from perspective projection?
column2: Affine transformations (translation, rotation, scaling, shearing) preserve parallel lines; perspective projection is non-affine because it introduces division that can make parallel lines converge.

column1: List the sequence of coordinate spaces a vertex passes through from model to screen.
column2: Object/Model space → World space → View (camera) space → Clip space → (after perspective divide) Normalized Device Coordinates → Screen space.

column1: What is the core invariant that makes modern rasterization 'order-independent' at the per-pixel level?
column2: The depth buffer (z-buffer): each pixel stores the closest fragment's depth seen so far, and a new fragment only overwrites color/depth if it is closer, regardless of submission order.

column1: In the rasterization pipeline, what two operations must occur after a triangle's vertices are projected to 2D screen points?
column2: (1) Determine which pixels fall inside the triangle (rasterization/coverage test), and (2) interpolate depth, color, and attribute values across the triangle's surface for each covered pixel.

column1: What was the Phong reflection model (1975) designed to achieve, and what was it NOT designed to be?
column2: It was engineered to look visually convincing and run fast on 1970s hardware using diffuse + specular terms; it was never intended to be physically accurate.

column1: What is the key philosophical difference between Phong shading and Physically-Based Rendering (PBR)?
column2: Phong uses arbitrary tweakable parameters chosen to look good; PBR grounds material properties (roughness, metallic, base reflectivity) in measured real-world data via a BRDF, so materials look consistent across different lighting environments.

column1: What does a BRDF mathematically describe?
column2: The Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function describes how light reflects off a surface as a function of the incoming light direction and the outgoing (viewing) direction.

column1: Why is normal mapping used instead of modeling true geometric surface detail?
column2: Normal mapping perturbs the surface normal per-pixel using a texture to simulate fine detail (e.g., wrinkles) that would otherwise require millions of extra polygons, giving the lighting appearance of detail cheaply.

column1: What is the 'hierarchical rejection principle' in spatial acceleration structures?
column2: Eliminating large groups of primitives through cheap containment tests (e.g., sphere/box-plane intersection) before invoking expensive per-triangle rasterization, discarding whole branches of invisible scene geometry early.

column1: Differentiate frustum culling, occlusion culling, and LOD selection.
column2: Frustum culling rejects objects outside the camera's view pyramid; occlusion culling rejects geometry hidden behind closer opaque objects; LOD selection swaps in simpler meshes for distant objects based on screen-space coverage.

column1: Why do thousands of individual draw calls hurt performance even if total triangle count is unchanged?
column2: Each draw call has fixed CPU/API overhead (state validation, descriptor binding, hardware scheduling) independent of triangle count, so many small draw calls bottleneck on overhead rather than GPU throughput; batching/instancing avoids this.
